1. Core Clinical Tension: A 52-year-old Chinese immigrant presenting with fever, worsening knee pain, and active synovitis across multiple joints (elbow, wrist, knee, ankle) with dactylitis. His knee swelling was previously misdiagnosed as DVT (leading to warfarin anticoagulation and bleeding) and hemarthrosis. With elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 44, ESR 62), mild fever (37.8°C), and negative serologies (RF, anti-CCP, HIV), his condition closely mimics seronegative spondyloarthropathy or acute polyarticular bacterial septic arthritis. The diagnosis of multi-focal tuberculous osteomyelitis/arthritis is notoriously delayed due to indolent progression and normal chest radiography.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical triage captures the history of five years of asymmetrical polyarthritis, recent knee hemarthrosis washout, worsening knee pain, and fever on representation. Vitals show temperature 37.8°C; physical exam reveals active synovitis of the right elbow, right wrist, left knee, left ankle, and dactylitis of the left middle PIP. Initial triage labs: mild anemia (Hb 10.0 g/dL), normal leukocyte and neutrophil counts, ESR 62 mm/hr, CRP 44 mg/L, normal chest X-ray, normal urinalysis, negative RF, negative anti-CCP, and negative HIV. The breakpoint stops before repeat arthrocentesis, empiric IV flucloxacillin, pelvic MRI, CT, and synovial biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute bacterial septic arthritis usually involves an acute monoarthritis, but can be polyarticular; however, it typically features marked leukocytosis and rapid purulent destruction, whereas this patient showed normal WBC and failed 2 weeks of high-dose flucloxacillin. Seronegative spondyloarthropathy / psoriatic arthritis presents with dactylitis and asymmetrical polyarthritis with negative RF/anti-CCP, but persistent fevers and granulomatous synovial histology dispute idiopathic autoimmune arthropathy. Sarcoidosis presents with granulomatous arthritis and hilar lymphadenopathy, but culture positivity definitively identifies mycobacterial infection.
case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man of Chinese descent who recently immigrated to the United Kingdom represents to the hospital with a two-week history of fever and worsening left knee pain. Two weeks earlier, he had been evaluated for over-anticoagulation following warfarin therapy, which had been empirically initiated at another facility under the suspicion of deep vein thrombosis for three months of left leg and knee swelling. During that prior evaluation, an ultrasound-guided knee aspiration revealed hemarthrosis, for which joint washout was performed; initial routine synovial fluid microscopy and bacterial cultures were negative. Upon further history obtained via a trained medical interpreter, he reports a five-year history of recurrent, asymmetrical polyarthritis prior to his migration.

On physical examination, he is mildly pyrexial with a temperature of 37.8°C. Musculoskeletal examination demonstrates swollen, warm, and tender joints involving the right elbow, right wrist, left knee, and left ankle, consistent with active synovitis. He also has dactylitis of the left middle proximal interphalangeal joint.

Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a mild anemia with a hemoglobin of 10.0 g/dL, a normal white blood cell count, and a normal neutrophil count. Inflammatory markers are elevated, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 62 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 44 mg/L. Serum rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies are negative. Urinalysis is normal. Screening for HIV is negative. A plain chest radiograph demonstrates no active pulmonary lesions or abnormalities.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given acute febrile joint worsening and marked systemic inflammatory markers, leading to an empiric trial of high-dose intravenous flucloxacillin; however, the patient failed to respond, fevers recurred, and routine bacterial cultures remained negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A differential diagnosis of polyarticular septic arthritis had been considered and intravenous flucloxacillin two grams every six hours was initiated on the advice of the Microbiologist. The fever settled initially and there was a minimal improvement in his inflammatory markers. The intravenous antibiotic was continued for two weeks but there was no further improvement in his inflammatory markers and his fever returned.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the 5-year history of recurrent asymmetrical polyarthritis, dactylitis, and negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, but pelvic MRI showed no sacroiliitis and synovial biopsy demonstrated granulomatous change rather than autoimmune synovitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: the possible alternative diagnosis of seronegative inflammatory arthritis was re-considered. Further investigations including a computerised tomographic (CT) scan of his chest and abdomen did not show any obvious pathology apart from small volume hilar lymphadenopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of his pelvis and sacroiliac joints showed no evidence of sacroilitis or a psoas abscess.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered when synovial tissue histology demonstrated granulomatous changes alongside small-volume hilar lymphadenopathy on thoracic imaging, but excluded by the ultimate isolation of viable mycobacteria from synovial cultures.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The Orthopaedic team performed a synovial biopsy from his knee. The result showed granulomatous changes and the synovial tissue was sent for polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Sarcoidosis and tuberculosis were suggested as possible differential diagnosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point occurred after prolonged 8-week incubation of the initial synovial fluid aspirate, which yielded Mycobacterium tuberculosis, while an isotope bone scan demonstrated multi-focal inflammatory uptake across multiple joints and ribs.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: After eight weeks in hospital, mycobacterium tuberculosis was grown from the initial synovial fluid sample taken from the knee. An isotope bone scan was performed and it has shown an increased uptake at the wrist, ribs, knees and ankles consistent with inflammatory changes. A diagnosis of multi-focal tuberculous osteomyelitis was made

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case for multi-focal tuberculous osteomyelitis masquerading as seronegative arthritis and septic arthritis. Admission breakpoint established prior to repeat synovial sampling and empiric antibiotics.
